title: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
hook: a plate heaped with rice, and a stone hidden under it: the Kashmiri poet Lal Ded, and the one word her teacher gave her
carry: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women
tomorrow: Lal Ded — a season of the tradition's women

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akka Mahadevi, asking for her alms to fall and a dog to take them, and ending on the lord white as jasmine. What did you find still in your hands? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

Dinner is served, and the young wife's plate looks generous, a full mound of rice. Only she knows what's underneath: a stone, with the rice spread thin over it, so the plate looks full while there's hardly anything to eat. That's a story Kashmiris tell about a young bride named Lalla and the mother-in-law who, tradition says, served her this way. In the story she doesn't complain. She eats what there is, washes the stone, and sets it back. In time she would leave that house and become the poet Kashmir remembers as Lal Ded.
screen: `A FULL PLATE OF RICE.` → `A STONE UNDERNEATH.` → `THE BRIDE WHO BECAME LAL DED.`

segments.voice: Lal Ded goes by more than one name. Lalla. Lalleshwari. Lal Ded, the name Kashmir knows her by best. She sang in Kashmiri, not in Sanskrit, in short sayings called vakhs, easy to remember and pass from mouth to mouth. The stories say that after years of hardship at home she left and walked out as a wandering seeker, and that she found a teacher. Then comes a saying about that teacher, here in paraphrase. My teacher gave me only one word. He said: from outside, go within. That one word became my rule, and so I began to dance, with nothing on. Notice how little she was given. Not a library. Not a long course of rituals. One word. And notice what she did with it. She didn't argue with it or add to it. She took it all the way. If what matters is within, then the outside, even the clothes, stops being the point. The story of the stone fits. A plate that looks full and isn't. A bride who knows exactly what's under the rice, and keeps quiet, because what feeds her isn't on the plate. Some readers hear her saying as a teaching about Shiva, found inside, the way some Shaiva teachers in Kashmir speak of him. Others hear a plainer lesson: a woman with almost nothing who turned that nothing into freedom. Year three gave a first glimpse of Lal Ded searching far and finding at home. This season, four days with her. Today, the one word.
screen: `A POET OF MANY NAMES` · `SHORT SAYINGS IN KASHMIRI` · `ONE WORD: GO WITHIN` · `WHAT'S UNDER THE RICE`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one word, turned inward. Sit, and let the breath slow. Notice where your attention is pointing right now: at sounds, at the screen, at the next thing to do. Then, gently, turn it around. From outside, in. Feel the breath at the tip of the nose, then in the chest. When the mind runs back outside, and it will, simply turn it in again. That turning is the whole practice. If you pray, you can look for God there, within, in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Lal Ded. The Kashmiri poet whose teacher gave her one word, from outside, go within, and who took it all the way. Today's word.

Your line: Lal Ded, a season of the tradition's women. Today, take one piece of advice you've been given, just one, and follow it all the way instead of collecting more. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-three.

what it means: in Lal Ded's saying, her teacher gives her one word: from outside, go within.
what a scholar hears: a whole path folded into one instruction, and a poet who answers it with her life rather than with more words.

notes: The stone-under-the-rice story is a traditional legend, told here as such; confirm its usual shape (stone covered with rice, Lalla washing it and returning it).

Vakh paraphrase: confirm against Grierson and Barnett's Lalla-Vakyani (the guru's single precept, 'from without enter within', and her dancing naked). Not quoted because the exact 1920 wording could not be verified.
'Lal Ded, which tradition hears as Granny Lal': confirm the gloss of 'Ded' (grandmother/elder woman).
The link to Kashmir's Shaiva teachers is kept general; a Keeper may want to name Kashmir Shaivism more precisely or leave it out.
howItsDone says she is remembered by Kashmiris of more than one faith (Hindu Lalleshwari, Muslim Lalla Arifa); confirm wording.
Original: लल्लेश्वरी (Lalleshwari) in Devanagari; confirm spelling. Kashmiri has also been written in Sharada and Perso-Arabic scripts.
Editor pass: cut the 'Granny Lal' gloss of Ded (etymology), 'one of her best-known sayings' (superlative), and told the stone story as story; softened the Kashmir Shaiva attribution.
